title: Design a Logging Framework — Logger, LogLevel (DEBUG/INFO/WARN/ERROR), Appender (console/file/remote), Formatter, singleton logger, thread safety.
topicTitle: LLD Problems — Parking Lot, Elevator, Chess, etc.

s1_definition.profdef: A logging framework design models a Logger that accepts messages at various levels, filters by a configured threshold, formats them through a Formatter, and writes them through one or more Appenders to destinations like console, file, or a remote service. It commonly uses the Singleton for shared loggers and must be thread safe.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the logging framework as the audit department at National Bank of India. Every action Rajesh takes is reported; the department decides which reports are important enough to keep (level threshold), stamps each with a standard header (formatter), and files copies to several places — a local binder, a central archive, and a monitoring desk (appenders). Many tellers report at once, so the filing must be orderly and safe (thread safety).
s1_definition.oneliner: A logging framework filters by level, formats the message, and fans it out to multiple appenders, safely across threads.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A logging framework design models a Logger that accepts messages at various levels, filters by a configured threshold, formats them through a Formatter, and writes them through one or more Appenders to destinations like console, file, or a remote service. It commonly uses the Singleton for shared loggers and must be thread safe.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the logging framework as the audit department at National Bank of India. Every action Rajesh takes is reported; the department decides which reports are important enough to keep (level threshold), stamps each with a standard header (formatter), and files copies to several places — a local binder, a central archive, and a monitoring desk (appenders). Many tellers report at once, so the filing must be orderly and safe (thread safety).

**One line to remember:** A logging framework filters by level, formats the message, and fans it out to multiple appenders, safely across threads.

sections.s2_technical:
The `Logger` holds a minimum `LogLevel` threshold; a message below the threshold is discarded cheaply. Levels are ordered DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR. An `Appender` interface abstracts the destination, with `ConsoleAppender`, `FileAppender`, and `RemoteAppender` implementations, so adding a destination is a new class — Open/Closed and Strategy combined.

A `Formatter` turns a level, timestamp, and message into a line. The Logger delegates formatting to it, so changing the layout never touches the Logger. A `LoggerFactory` hands out loggers, often cached per name as a Singleton so the whole application shares configuration.

```java
logger.info(() -> "Transfer " + amount + " from " + from);
```

I pass messages as a supplier lambda so the string is built only if the level is enabled, avoiding wasted work. Thread safety matters because many threads log concurrently; appenders must synchronize their writes or use a lock-free queue, and in high-throughput banking systems I use an asynchronous appender backed by a ring buffer so logging never blocks the business thread.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Across National Bank of India, every service logs transfers and errors, and these must go to both the console during development and a file in production, with the level threshold controlling the noise. This is exactly the appender and level-threshold design.

Problem 2 — Many transfer threads log at the same instant, and the log file must not get garbled. This is exactly the thread-safety concern.

The code defines `LogLevel`, an `Appender` interface with console and file implementations, a `Formatter`, and a thread-safe `Logger` from a factory, with a demo logging an info and a filtered debug message.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a logger for TransferService at INFO threshold with console and file appenders, logging one info and one debug message.

Step 1: `LoggerFactory.get` creates the logger once and caches it, so later calls with the same name reuse it. Step 2: `log.info` sees INFO is at or above the INFO threshold, so it builds the line through the formatter and fans it out to both the console and the file appender, each writing under its own lock. Step 3: `log.debug` sees DEBUG is below INFO, so it returns immediately without even building the string. Step 4: the file appender's contents show only the info line.

```
2026-10-31T22:17 [INFO] TransferService - Transfer 50000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001 (Rajesh→Priya)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  log.info(() -> "Transfer 50000 ...")
     │ level INFO ≥ threshold INFO
     ▼
  Formatter.format → "...[INFO] TransferService - ..."
     │ fan out
     ├─▶ ConsoleAppender.append (sync)
     └─▶ FileAppender.append (sync)

  log.debug(...) : DEBUG < INFO → discarded (string never built)
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Logging Framework ═══

  ┌─ Patterns ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Singleton: LoggerFactory caches loggers           │
  │ Strategy: Appender (console/file/remote)          │
  │ Strategy: Formatter (plain/JSON)                  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: Logger filters; Appender writes; Formatter fmts│
  │ O: new destination = new Appender                 │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────┐ uses ┌────────────┐
  │   Logger     │─────▶│ Formatter  │
  │ - threshold  │      └────────────┘
  │ - appenders  │◇── Appender (interface) *
  │ + info/debug │        ├─ ConsoleAppender
  └──────────────┘        ├─ FileAppender
                          └─ RemoteAppender
  ┌──────────────┐ caches
  │ LoggerFactory│──────▶ Logger (singleton per name)
  └──────────────┘

  Call Chain:
  1. factory.get(name) → cached Logger
  2. info(supplier): filter → format → each appender.append()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When I design a logging framework, I separate four responsibilities so each can evolve independently. The Logger decides whether a message passes the configured level threshold, the Formatter decides how a line looks, the Appender decides where it goes, and a LoggerFactory hands out loggers that share configuration. This separation is what lets a framework support console in development and file plus remote in production without rewriting the core.

Levels are ordered from debug up to error, and the Logger holds a minimum threshold so anything below it is discarded cheaply. A key efficiency trick I always use is accepting the message as a supplier lambda, so the string is only built when the level is actually enabled — in a hot transfer path, building log strings that get thrown away is pure waste.

The Appender is an interface with implementations for console, file, and remote destinations, which is the Strategy pattern, so adding a new sink like a database or Kafka is a new class rather than a change to the Logger. The Formatter is pluggable the same way, so switching from plain text to structured JSON logs is a configuration choice.

Thread safety is non-negotiable because in a banking system many transfer threads log at the same instant, and the log file must never get garbled. I synchronize appender writes, and in high-throughput services I move to an asynchronous appender backed by a ring buffer so the business thread never blocks on I/O. The senior insight I bring is that logging must be both cheap when disabled and safe under heavy concurrency, which is exactly why I rely on lazy message suppliers and lock-free async appenders in the services I run at National Bank of India.
